source.title: STEM: Scaling Transformers with Embedding Modules
source.authors: Ranajoy Sadhukhan; Sheng Cao; Harry Dong; Changsheng Zhao; Attiano Purpura-Pontoniere; Yuandong Tian; Ze-Chun Liu; Bei-Di Chen

record.tranche_reason: The study reports validation perplexity across training tokens for dense and STEM models, but does not fit or test the original scaling-law equations.
record.gate_note: Figure 1a reports validation PPL versus training tokens for 1B dense and STEM models, and the text says STEM achieves lower validation loss. The study does not report fitted power laws or assess whether small-run fits predict larger runs. Its training-loss plots against tokens and FLOPs are not held-out loss, so they are not rows for these claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study is an architecture paper proposing STEM, a token-indexed sparse FFN. It cites Kaplan et al. and Hoffmann et al. only as motivation for sparse parameter scaling. It fits no power law, sweeps no model size or compute for held-out loss, tests no extrapolation or allocation, and runs no shape-at-fixed-parameter ablation. Figure 1a shows one training curve each for a 1B dense and a 1B STEM model. That comparison is between architectures, not a test of any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right but too narrow. The authors conclude that STEM trains stably compared with fine-grained MoE and improves downstream accuracy over dense baselines (up to ~3–4%) with fewer per-token FLOPs. They also report lower training and validation loss, more interpretable knowledge editing, and better long-context performance. They draw no conclusion about power-law scaling.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares a token-indexed sparse FFN design with dense and Hash-MoE baselines; it does not reproduce the original scaling-law fitting or compute-optimal allocation procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports that replacing the FFN up-projection with STEM performs better than replacing the gate projection, but this is an architectural ablation rather than a sensitivity test of fitted scaling laws.

fits_no_version.finding: Replacing the FFN up-projection with token-indexed embedding tables raises total parameters while lowering active FLOPs. This gives lower training and validation loss and higher downstream accuracy than dense baselines. Replacing more layers lowers training loss at fewer FLOPs (Fig. 5b; Table 3 ROI 1.08x/1.20x/1.33x).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Static token-indexed sparse parameters can deliver parameter-scaling benefits in loss without proportional per-token compute.

record.problems: The relevant validation-loss comparison is shown as a plot without reported fitted exponents or numerical loss values; no uncertainty is reported for it.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 5a and Figure 5b report training loss versus training tokens and FLOPs, respectively, not held-out pretraining loss. They are therefore omitted.

untested.parts: Power-law form of held-out loss in parameters, tokens or compute is not fitted or examined.
No shape ablation at fixed parameter count. STEM variants change total and active parameter counts.
No non-text or other-regime scaling fits.
Only two model scales (350M, 1B) of different architectures. Downstream scores are not related to scale or loss as a trend.
No comparison of fitting choices or exponents.

record.verdict_notes: The training-loss figures (5a, 5b) are correctly left out. Even as held-out loss they would be architecture comparisons, not scaling-law tests. The reader's 'tests'/T2 classification is overturned to cites_only/T6.

versions.untested_parts: The power-law functional form is not fitted or assessed; no sweeps over parameter count or compute for held-out loss are reported.
